issues.description: The manuscript contains a sentence claiming findings generalize to mixed-gender collaborative settings, but the study exclusively used sex-segregated chains (all-male or all-female). No mixed-gender chains were tested, making this claim entirely unsupported by the data. This sentence appears to be inserted without any empirical or logical basis from the study design.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.description: Chains were exclusively male or exclusively female, but no rationale is provided for this design choice. This introduces a potential confound (gender effects) that is never analyzed or discussed. If gender has no effect, why segregate? If it might, the design should test for it. The design prevents any assessment of whether cultural transmission operates similarly across genders or in mixed-gender groups.
issues.quote: participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females)

issues.description: No power analysis or formal sample size determination was conducted. The justification is simply that sample sizes exceed those of previous publications, which is not a valid basis for ensuring adequate statistical power, particularly for detecting treatment differences (the key comparison between Configurations and Configurations + Theory).
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications

issues.description: By generation 5, average speed (145.7 m/h) approaches the theoretical maximum (~154 m/h), leaving only ~8.3 m/h room for improvement. This ceiling effect could mask real treatment differences in rate of optimization. The wide confidence interval for the treatment effect (−10.76, 18.13) suggests the study may be underpowered to detect meaningful differences between treatments, especially with this compressed range.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.description: The claim of '71% optimization' is not clearly defined. It is unclear what baseline is being used. Generation 1 already achieved ~123.6 m/h (80% of maximum), so the cultural transmission added ~22 m/h. The 71% figure could mislead readers into thinking the improvement from cultural transmission was much larger than it was. The calculation method should be explicitly stated.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.description: In the Configurations + Theory treatment, participants both received AND wrote theories. The act of formulating an explicit theory could itself affect exploration behavior and understanding (a testing/generation effect), independent of receiving a theory. This confounds the effects of writing a theory with receiving one, making it impossible to isolate which aspect drives the observed effects on exploration and understanding.
issues.quote: participants additionally received the previous participant's theory about the physical system. Participants were asked to write their theory before the test phase was completed.

issues.description: The understanding test uses 10 forced-choice comparisons of wheel pairs, with only 5 items per dimension. With 3 response options per item, the test has limited range (0-10, chance ~3.33) and likely low reliability, potentially failing to detect genuine changes in understanding across generations. This low measurement sensitivity could lead to a false negative conclusion that understanding does not improve.
issues.quote: The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

issues.subcategory: fixed order of understanding test items
issues.description: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order. This introduces potential order effects (e.g., fatigue, learning, anchoring) that could systematically bias understanding scores. Counterbalancing or randomization of item order would be needed to rule out this confound.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.description: Both data collection and data analysis were conducted without blinding to experimental conditions. The experimenter physically set up the wheel for each trial and could see the participant's condition. This creates potential for experimenter demand effects, particularly since the experimenter could inadvertently behave differently across conditions.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.description: The preregistered model for analysis 4 did not converge, and the authors modified their analysis by aggregating scores and removing terms. While they explain the rationale (negative correlation between inertia and CoM scores), non-convergence of a preregistered model may indicate model misspecification or data issues that should be explored further. The negative correlation itself is theoretically interesting and potentially undermines the aggregated score approach, since aggregation masks opposing patterns.
issues.quote: the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable "Physical Principle" in the reported model.

issues.description: Inertia and centre-of-mass understanding scores are negatively correlated, yet the primary analysis uses an aggregated total score. This aggregation can mask meaningful changes: if theory transmission increases understanding of one dimension while decreasing understanding of the other, the aggregate score would show no change. This is acknowledged in the text but the primary analysis still uses the aggregate, potentially leading to false null results.
issues.quote: analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated

issues.description: The understanding measure tests whether participants can predict relative speeds of wheel pairs, which may capture pattern recognition or implicit knowledge rather than explicit causal understanding. A participant could score well by recognizing 'weights close to center = faster' without understanding the causal mechanism (moment of inertia). The paper's strong claims about absence of 'causal understanding' may not be warranted by this measure.
issues.quote: A participant who understands the effects of varying the moment of inertia should predict that a wheel with 4 weights close to the axis would cover the track quicker than a wheel with 4 weights farther from the axis

issues.description: The authors acknowledge the task is a conservative test because it is low-dimensional (2 variables), yet they draw strong conclusions about complex real-world technologies like bows and kayaks. A 2D optimization problem may be fundamentally different from the many-dimensional problems the cultural niche hypothesis addresses. The results may not scale to higher-dimensional problems where individual understanding might play a more critical role.
issues.quote: the optimization problem is low-dimensional, which provides a conservative test of our hypotheses, compared to the many-dimensional problem of optimizing, for example, the performance of a bow

issues.description: Chains of only 5 generations may be insufficient to observe divergence between treatments or detect improvements in understanding. Real cumulative cultural evolution operates over many more generations. The ceiling effect at generation 5 suggests the task may have been too easy to require more than a few generations, limiting the study's ability to address the central question about the role of causal understanding in long-term cultural evolution.
issues.quote: Participants were organized into chains of 5 individuals.

issues.description: Only the last two configurations and scores were transmitted between generations. This is a narrow bottleneck that may underrepresent the richness of real cultural transmission. With more transmitted information (e.g., all 5 trials and their outcomes), participants might develop better causal models. This design choice biases the study toward finding that understanding doesn't improve.
issues.quote: All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain so as to simulate overlapping generations.

issues.description: The handling of failed wheels (those that did not descend) differs across analyses. In Analysis 1, data are restricted to last two trials to limit failures. In Analysis 3, failures are assigned speed = 0. These different approaches could lead to inconsistent conclusions across analyses and make cross-analysis comparisons problematic.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.

issues.description: The sample consists entirely of French university students. The authors acknowledge this limitation and call for cross-cultural work, but the strong conclusions about human cultural evolution and the cognitive niche hypothesis are not well-supported by a single WEIRD population. The participants' intuitions may be heavily influenced by formal physics education or Western cultural experience with wheels.
issues.quote: we asked successive 'cultural generations' of participants (French university students) to optimize a physical system

issues.subcategory: small subgroup sample sizes in exploratory analyses
issues.description: The exploratory analyses examining effects of different theory types involve very small subgroups: 15 (inertia theory), 17 (CoM theory), 6 (full theory), and 18 (irrelevant theories). The full theory group (N=6) is especially small, yet heat maps and conclusions are drawn from these groups. These results are likely underpowered and unreliable.
issues.quote: 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories

issues.subcategory: exploratory analyses presented as primary findings
issues.description: While labeled as 'exploratory,' the analyses of theory-type effects on exploration and understanding are given central prominence (Figure 3, substantial text in results and discussion). These non-preregistered findings drive key conclusions about the canalizing effect of theory transmission, yet they lack the confirmatory rigor needed for such emphasis.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants' exploration behavior

issues.description: Understanding was measured only after participants completed their 5 trials. Without a pre-task measure, it is impossible to determine whether participants' understanding changed as a result of the task or was pre-existing. The claim that understanding 'did not improve over generations' is based on between-subject comparisons across generations, but individual changes in understanding cannot be assessed.
issues.quote: Participants' understanding was evaluated after they completed their 5 trials by asking them to predict which of two wheels would cover the distance faster

issues.description: Theories were constrained to start with 'The wheel covers the distance faster when...' and had a 340-character limit. This format may have prevented participants from expressing more nuanced, multidimensional, or process-based causal theories. The finding that theories were mostly unidimensional could partly be an artifact of these format constraints.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with "The wheel covers the distance faster when...".

issues.subcategory: theory transmission confounded with information restriction
issues.description: Participants in the theory treatment were explicitly prevented from transmitting information about specific configuration performance in their theories, to maintain equivalence with the Configurations treatment. However, this restriction means theories could not include the most directly useful quantitative information, potentially reducing the effectiveness of theory transmission artificially.
issues.quote: Participants could not transmit information about the performance of a specific configuration in order to prevent individuals from extending the number of transmitted configurations as compared to the "Configurations" treatment.

issues.subcategory: absence of evidence vs. evidence of absence
issues.description: The study interprets the lack of a treatment difference (wide CI spanning zero for Treatment effect: −10.76, 18.13) as evidence that theory transmission has 'no noticeable effect.' This is a classic error of treating non-significant results as evidence for the null hypothesis. With Bayesian methods, a Bayes factor or explicit model comparison for the null would be more appropriate for supporting this claim.
issues.quote: these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding

issues.description: The results section reports generation 1 speeds based on 'last trial' for descriptive statistics, while the formal statistical analysis (Analysis 1) uses 'last two trials.' This inconsistency makes it unclear what exactly is being compared and could lead to discrepancies between descriptive and inferential results.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h

issues.description: Participants were told their payoff depended on both their own performance and the next participant's performance, and that their last two configurations would be transmitted. This creates demand characteristics encouraging conservative strategies on late trials (to ensure transmittable good configurations) rather than exploratory strategies. This could artificially suppress exploration in later trials and bias toward incremental improvement.
issues.quote: their reward depended both on their own performance and on the performance of the next participant in their chain

issues.description: The experimenter manually positioned the weights on the physical wheel according to the participant's configuration. This introduces potential for small positioning errors and for the experimenter to inadvertently influence outcomes. The experimenter could see the condition and configuration, creating opportunities for unconscious bias in weight placement precision.
issues.quote: Once the configuration was confirmed by the participant, the experimenter positioned the weights on the physical wheel accordingly

issues.description: The main text describes the models in general terms but refers to supplementary tables for full model outputs. Key details such as prior specifications for the Bayesian models, number of chains, iterations, convergence diagnostics (e.g., Rhat values), and effective sample sizes are not reported in the main text, making it difficult to evaluate the reliability of the statistical results.
issues.quote: Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.description: For Analysis 1, the authors state 'The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.' This post-hoc model selection based on fit could lead to overfitting and was apparently not preregistered. The criteria for model comparison (e.g., WAIC, LOO) are not specified.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.description: Theory coding used a binary classification (contains inertia info yes/no, contains CoM info yes/no) by 3 coders. While inter-rater reliability was good (κ = 0.81, 0.85), the coarse categorization may miss important nuances in theory quality, specificity, or accuracy. A theory mentioning inertia vaguely vs. precisely would be coded the same way.
issues.quote: 3 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel and were asked to code participants' theories according to whether they contain accurate information related to moment of inertia and/or centre of mass.

issues.description: There is a typographic/grammatical error in the methods section ('Data collection and was not performed blind'), suggesting incomplete editing that could indicate other unreported oversights.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: conflation of individual and cultural learning
issues.description: Generation 1 participants already achieve substantial performance (123.6 m/h out of ~154 m/h maximum) through individual trial-and-error within 5 trials. The additional cultural accumulation is relatively modest (123.6 to 145.7 m/h). The strong claims about cultural accumulation producing 'highly optimized solutions' may overstate the contribution of cultural transmission relative to individual learning.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h...After 5 generations, average wheel speed increased to 145.7 m/h

issues.subcategory: no control condition without cultural transmission
issues.description: There is no control condition in which participants attempt the task without any social information (i.e., isolated individuals across all generations). Without this baseline, it is difficult to quantify how much of the generation-over-generation improvement is due to cultural transmission versus what any naive participant could achieve with 5 trials. Generation 1 serves as a partial control but does not account for potential time/session effects.
issues.quote: All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain
